This is the beginning of the story I wrote last night/this morning based on the two Image Prompts on this subverse, The North Watch posted by ST and The South Watch posted by me. I really like the overall idea, and just decided to put up the first part if anyone is interested.

The wall stood between the snow below and the skies above like a giant wave of frozen stone. And between the top of the wall and the bottom of the sky there was Finbar.

Somewhere above Finbar’s head, the wind was gathering strength, making him shiver. The tiny specks of snow and ice were starting to fly around him, obscuring the view and almost extinguishing the torch he held in his hand. He huddled closer to the parapet and sat down in the knee-deep snow.

Finbar was shaking. It was getting harder every night. It was hard being old. It was hard pushing through the snow on top of a ruined wall in the middle of nowhere. It was hard getting up, and it was hard sitting down. It was hard to keep on moving.

Finbar breathed in, and he breathed out. The moist air turned to a whiff of white and then flew away, far into the darkness beyond the parapet. The wind was howling, and Finbar was waiting for something. Perhaps he was waiting for spring to come.

The next morning, the three remaining members of the Wall Watch stood around a body of the man lying down, covered with a blanket of fresh snow. A quick prayer to No God, a moment of silence, and then a strong push. The sound of a body hitting the ground below never came, swallowed by the snow storm, stolen by the air and the skies.

The sun was rising. The three figures looked towards the horizon for a moment, covering their eyes against the ice needles flying through the air, and then, as if awoken from a deep sleep, exchanged a few quick glances and started walking away along the wall’s ridge. It was time for breakfast.

Breakfast consisted of bread that had to be thrown into boiling water to stop resembling a grey brick in colour and consistency, a bit of dry meat, and whatever remained of the supplies that were rationed for the forth, now forever absent, member of the company. They ate in silence. Snow was falling somewhere above their heads, spiralling and weighing down the tent’s roof. Smoke was slowly filling up the small space, clinging to the bodies and the clothes, as if trying to warm itself up against the cold air.

‘I’ve got to go down, see if we can find some firewood’. The words coming from a dry throat cut the silence, making the others turn.

Rory stood up with his head bowed as to not hit the ceiling, not looking at his companions, and walked out without another word. Niall shot an apologetic smile to Irya and shuffled uneasily.

‘Go on,’ she said. ‘Follow him. I don’t want to see him falling off the wall as well, do you?’

Niall half-smiled once more, and left, leaving the tent’s door flapping softly in the wind. Irya looked at it moving to and fro for a while and then closed her eyes. When she opened them again, tears were slowly running down her face. With the back of her hand, she wiped them off, shifted in her seat, and stayed there, immobile, looking at the tiny flames dancing, listening to the wind.

It was colder outside now that he was accustomed to the warmth of the refuge, Niall thought to himself. It was always cold here though. It was hard remembering a time here that wasn’t winter. Niall took a deep breath, and then made his way towards the staircase that led down, towards the ground far below. He hooked up his ropes next to where Rory put his, closed his eyes for a second, and then began the journey, trying at all costs to avoid the huge gaping holes in the steps.

Niall hated going down. In fact, the only thing he hated more than going down was going up. It was always the same, the horrifying emptiness of air just inches away from him, the pain in his muscles as he tried to cling closer to the wall, the cold in his fingers. He had long ago decided that no pay was worth this, and every week he wanted to leave, to pack up his measly belongings and walk across the frozen plain. The only thing stopping him was the fact that no man could cross three hundred parra that separated the Wall from the next settlement alone, and so every week he stayed.

In what felt like hours, Niall had finally managed to get down. Here, on the ground, the thick layer of snow made it almost impossible to travel without the old pair of snow boots. Niall sighed and began walking, following Rory’s footsteps, suddenly very aware that a body was lying just a couple of meters away from, somewhere on the other side of the cold stone. He shivered.

Somewhere on the other side of the Wall, there was indeed a dead body, looking up to the sky with its dead eyes, waiting for spring to come. Somewhere on that other side of the Wall, many parra away, there were also many more bodies very much alive, standing shoulder to shoulder, waiting for a command.

And the command came.

The Tenth Imperial Army started moving across the Northern Plains, slowly gaining speed and momentum, moving like a giant wave of human flesh and metal. The Tenth Imperial Army began their march towards the Conrí Wall.
